To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific.

Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey.

Participants provided informed consent and were given instructions for the task.

We sampled N = 310 participants (49.7% female), aged 19-85 (MAge = 45.9) from Prolific in a preregistered study with a representative sample from the US population: https://osf.io/ymzqc/overview?view_only=b9463362065e4965b0edd18a728fba9e.

After answering the Cringe Scale items, participants were randomly assigned between-subjects to a cringe or neutral scenario condition in which they received 10 short scenarios, 4 vignettes, and 4 short (around 1 minute) videos corresponding to their experimental condition.

We sampled N = 307 participants (51.8% female), aged 19-72 (MAge = 38.74) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2q73k/overview?view_only=4ecf65adc28d47ac9ea670175c3bc12b.

Participants were compensated $2.50 for participating in a 15-min survey.

To that end, participants completed our 20-item Cringe Scale from Study 2 as well as the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (VES; Uysal et al., 2014), which they received in a random order.

Participants were then randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral emotion condition between-subjects and saw five videos corresponding to their assigned condition in a fixed order.

Participants completed an incentivized donation task (i.e., a dictator game with the nonprofit as the recipient) after watching each of the nonprofit videos.

We tested N = 200 participants (53.0% female), aged 21-77 (MAge = 41.2) from Prolific.

Participants were compensated $1.85 for participating in a 10-min survey.

No participants were excluded from analysis.

Participants were assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment scenario condition between-subjects.

Participants were provided with a short, colloquial definition of their condition’s emotion (see Study 4 -Supplementary Materials for definition text) and were asked to generate three short example scenarios that best capture that emotion.

Doing so allowed us to capture lay perceptions of these two emotions and mitigate concerns that participants were anchoring their responses to the experimenter-provided definitions from Study 4.

We tested N = 405 participants (52.1% female), aged 18-80 (MAge = 44.8) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2u3wc/overview?view_only=af15f6d30a124aa0ac716212de0b79e0.

Participants were compensated $2.85 for participating in a 17-min survey.

Participants were randomly assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment condition, an intentional or accidental vignette condition, and to a public or private reputation condition, all between-subjects.

Participants were then asked to generate their own example scenario of cringe or vicarious embarrassment, depending on their condition assignment, and rated it on the same nine measures.

After the reputation vignettes, participants completed our 20item Cringe Scale.

power_id text
1 We tested N = 405 participants (52.1% female), aged 18-80 (MAge = 44.8) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2u3wc/overview?view_only=af15f6d30a124aa0ac716212de0b79e0. Participants were compensated $2.85 for participating in a 17-min survey. We initially recruited 416 participants, but 11 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria. Sample size was determined using a statistical power simulation with data from Study 4 which found we would have 100% power (95% CI: 99.63, 100%) to detect an effect of emotion condition with N = 400 given the effect size observed in Study 4 for the intent measure.
2 We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific. Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey. We conducted an a priori power calculation using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) in R to determine the number of participants needed to reject a model based on a root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) of 0.05, 169 degrees of freedom, 90% power, and an alpha of 0.05 (Jobst et al., 2023). The analysis suggested a minimum sample of 148 observations. We consequently oversampled to account for potential attrition due to failed attention checks or incomplete submissions.
3 Although we preregistered LMEMs controlling for the random intercepts of participant and vignette identity, after data analysis we determined that these models were underpowered for our central comparison between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. Because the two scenario conditions used different vignettes (five each), treating vignettes as a random factor meant that the condition effect is estimated from just 10 vignettes rather than from 405 participants (Judd et al., 2012). These tests are therefore very conservative and are powered to detect only large differences between the two sets of vignettes (approximately d ≥ 2.0; Westfall et al., 2014). We therefore deviated from our preregistration: We report LMEMs with a random intercept for participant ID here and report the preregistered models with crossed random intercepts for participant and vignette in the supplement (see Study 5 -Results). Because the two sets of models address different questions-whether participants distinguished our particular cringe and vicarious embarrassment vignettes, and whether these differences generalize to cringe and vicarious embarrassment scenarios more broadly-we discuss the results of both in the Study 5 Discussion.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 5 imprecise p values out of 86 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p-values > .88 Additionally, there was no interaction effect between Cringe Scale score and stimuli type (all interaction term p-values > .88; see Table S10), indicating that modality of the stimuli (e.g., video vs vignette) did not influence the relationship between cringe sensitivity and cringe perceptions. factor loadings from Study 2.
p ≤ .016 Punishment appropriateness Multivariate LMEM; Holmcorrected simple slopes Cringe Scale score × Punishment type Appropriateness of each punishment Higher trait cringe → active punishment more appropriate (B = 2.23-3.33, all p ≤ .016) Higher trait cringe → doing nothing less appropriate (B = -3.53***) What role does transgressor intent play?
ps ≥ .139 Differences in norm violation, moral wrongness, normative punishment judgments, and norm awareness were no longer significant (all ps ≥ .139), nor were the manipulation checks (ps ≥ .197); effects of the intent manipulation, trait cringe, and reputation condition were unchanged.
ps ≥ .197 Differences in norm violation, moral wrongness, normative punishment judgments, and norm awareness were no longer significant (all ps ≥ .139), nor were the manipulation checks (ps ≥ .197); effects of the intent manipulation, trait cringe, and reputation condition were unchanged.
p > 0.05 The Cringe Scale (B = 4.67, SE = 0.63, p < .001) and VES (B = 3.80, SE = 0.56, p < .001) were positively associated with cringe perceptions independently, but in a combined model only the Cringe Scale significantly predicted cringe perceptions (B = 3.56, SE = 1.16, p = 0.002) whereas VES did not (B = 1.16, SE = 1.02, p > 0.05).

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

README Files

README files are a way to document the contents and structure of a folder, helping users locate the information they need. You can use a README to document changes to a repository, and explain how files are named. Please consider adding a README to each repository or including ‘README’ in the name of your overview document.

Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 9 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (9). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a ._ copy of a .csv for data).

Remove these: Operating system files: macOS adds a __MACOSX folder and a ._ copy of every file it puts in a zip, and .DS_Store files to folders; Windows adds Thumbs.db and desktop.ini. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with zip -r -X, or remove them afterwards with zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store". RStudio session files (.Rproj.user/) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; R history (.Rhistory) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; Jupyter checkpoints (.ipynb_checkpoints/) are automatic copies of notebooks; compiled Python files (__pycache__/, .pyc) are recreated when the code runs; open-document lock files (~$...docx, .~lock...#) are left while a document is open; editor backups (file~, .bak, .swp) and temporary files (.tmp, .temp) are copies a program made by itself.

Keep only on purpose: version control folders (.git, .svn, .hg) hold the project’s history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; editor settings (.idea, .vscode) can hold paths on your own computer. A .gitignore based on GitHub’s templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 21 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

p = .22 This held true when separately examining behavioral intentions (LRT χ² (1) = 1.53, p = .22) and donation decisions (LRT χ² (1) = 0.63, p = .43).
p = .43 This held true when separately examining behavioral intentions (LRT χ² (1) = 1.53, p = .22) and donation decisions (LRT χ² (1) = 0.63, p = .43).
p = .09 However, when breaking up the Cringe Scale by its two latent factors, we found that the model including Vicarious Social Anxiety (B = 3.54, SE = 1.73, p = .04) and VES (B = 2.83, SE = 1.65, p = .09), explained significantly more variance in behavioral outcomes than a model with just VES (LRT χ² (1) = 4.20, p = .04), suggesting that the first factor of the Cringe Scale offers unique predictive validity over and above the VES.
p = .18 However, we found no difference between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in perceptions of humor (B = -5.00, SE = 3.35, p = .18), emotional valence (B = 0.53, SE = 2.36, p = .82), or relevance to social norms (B = 2.83, SE = 3.44, p = .46).
p = .82 However, we found no difference between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in perceptions of humor (B = -5.00, SE = 3.35, p = .18), emotional valence (B = 0.53, SE = 2.36, p = .82), or relevance to social norms (B = 2.83, SE = 3.44, p = .46).
p = .46 However, we found no difference between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in perceptions of humor (B = -5.00, SE = 3.35, p = .18), emotional valence (B = 0.53, SE = 2.36, p = .82), or relevance to social norms (B = 2.83, SE = 3.44, p = .46).
p = .16 There was no difference between scenario conditions in the appropriateness of no punishment (B = -2.37, SE = 1.68, p = .16).
p = .32 The Cringe Scale score did not significantly predict norm violation perceptions (B = 0.80, SE = 0.79, p = .32) but did significantly predict normative punishment judgments (B = 1.72, SE = 0.62, p = .006).
ps ≥ .139 Differences in norm violation, moral wrongness, normative punishment judgments, and norm awareness were no longer significant (all ps ≥ .139), nor were the manipulation checks (ps ≥ .197); effects of the intent manipulation, trait cringe, and reputation condition were unchanged.
ps ≥ .197 Differences in norm violation, moral wrongness, normative punishment judgments, and norm awareness were no longer significant (all ps ≥ .139), nor were the manipulation checks (ps ≥ .197); effects of the intent manipulation, trait cringe, and reputation condition were unchanged.
p = 0.31 However, the indirect effect of norm violation perceptions was not (B = 0.29, SE = 0.29, p = 0.31), indicating that perceptions of norm violation severity did not mediate the effect of trait cringe on cringe perceptions.
p > 0.05 The Cringe Scale (B = 4.67, SE = 0.63, p < .001) and VES (B = 3.80, SE = 0.56, p < .001) were positively associated with cringe perceptions independently, but in a combined model only the Cringe Scale significantly predicted cringe perceptions (B = 3.56, SE = 1.16, p = 0.002) whereas VES did not (B = 1.16, SE = 1.02, p > 0.05).

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code). All your code files had comments.

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 2 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 17 distinct packages/libraries: car, conflicted, corrplot, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, gt, lavaan, lavaanPlot, lme4, lmerTest, performance, psych, semPower, semTools, systemfit, tidyr. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 617 columns across 9 data files.

Issues Identified

49 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

169 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 8 of 9 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 6 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

Order File Runs after Basis
1 cringe.s1_osf_top.Rmd — numeric
2 cringe.s2_osf_top.Rmd — numeric
3 cringe.s3_osf_top.Rmd — numeric
4 cringe.s4_osf_top.Rmd — numeric
5 cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd — numeric
6 cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd — none

File paths

9 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv (in cringe.s3_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s5_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s5_osf.csv (in cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s5.wide_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s5.wide_osf.csv (in cringe.s5_osf_top.Rmd); cringe_combined.CFA_wide.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe_combined.CFA_wide.csv (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); cringe_combined.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe_combined.csv (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s3.wide_osf.csv (in cringe.combined_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s2_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s2_osf.csv (in cringe.s2_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s4_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s4_osf.csv (in cringe.s4_osf_top.Rmd); cringe.s1_osf.csv to ../../Cringe Data.zip/cringe.s1_osf.csv (in cringe.s1_osf_top.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 1 data path was built at runtime with sprintf()/paste()/file.path() instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author’s own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 6 scripts: 6 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

> library(gt)
> model_rows <- function(model, model.name, type) {
>   est <- coef(summary(model))
>   est <- est[rownames(est) != "(Intercept)", , drop = FALSE]
>   data.frame(Model     = paste0(model.name, " — ", type),
>              Predictor = rownames(est),
>              B         = est[, "Estimate"],
>              SE        = est[, "Std. Error"],
>              df        = est[, "df"],
>              t         = est[, "t value"],
>              p         = est[, "Pr(>|t|)"],
>              row.names = NULL)
> }

All models are linear mixed models with a random intercept for participant; <em>p</em> values use Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. Reference levels: neutral (condition), short scenarios (modality), not seen (prior viewing). Cringe Scale score is the average of the 20 items (1–7). Model 7 uses the cringe condition only (<em>n</em> = 156); Model 10 uses video ratings only. Each model is labeled preregistered or exploratory as described in the manuscript.</span></td>

> fit_flag <- function(formula, data) {
>   warns <- character(0)
>   m <- withCallingHandlers(
>     lmer(formula, data = data),
>     warning = function(w) { warns <<- c(warns, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
>   status <- if (length(warns) > 0) "convergence warning" else if (isSingular(m)) "singular fit" else "converged"
>   list(model = m, status = status)
> }
> sens.specs <- list(
>   list("Perceptions ~ Cringe Scale",             perc.long,   "response ~ cringe.score",                   "cringe.score",         NA),
>   list("Perceptions ~ VES",                      perc.long,   "response ~ VE.score",                       "VE.score",             NA),
>   list("Perceptions ~ VES + Cringe Scale",       perc.long,   "response ~ VE.score + cringe.score",        "cringe.score",         "response ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Perceptions ~ VES + Inauthenticity",     perc.long,   "response ~ VE.score + cringe.score_fake",   "cringe.score_fake",    "response ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Perceptions ~ VES + Vic. social anxiety",perc.long,   "response ~ VE.score + cringe.score_vic.anx","cringe.score_vic.anx", "response ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Behavior ~ Cringe Scale",                beh.long,    "behavior ~ cringe.score",                   "cringe.score",         NA),
>   list("Intentions ~ Cringe Scale",              intent.long, "behavior ~ cringe.score",                   "cringe.score",         NA),
>   list("Donations ~ Cringe Scale",               donate.long, "behavior ~ cringe.score",                   "cringe.score",         NA),
>   list("Behavior ~ Condition",                   beh.long,    "behavior ~ cond",                           "condcringe",           NA),
>   list("Intentions ~ Condition",                 intent.long, "behavior ~ cond",                           "condcringe",           NA),
>   list("Donations ~ Condition",                  donate.long, "behavior ~ cond",                           "condcringe",           NA),
>   list("Behavior ~ VES + Cringe Scale",          beh.long,    "behavior ~ VE.score + cringe.score",        "cringe.score",         "behavior ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Intentions ~ VES + Cringe Scale",        intent.long, "behavior ~ VE.score + cringe.score",        "cringe.score",         "behavior ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Donations ~ VES + Cringe Scale",         donate.long, "behavior ~ VE.score + cringe.score",        "cringe.score",         "behavior ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Behavior ~ VES + Vic. social anxiety",   beh.long,    "behavior ~ VE.score + cringe.score_vic.anx","cringe.score_vic.anx", "behavior ~ VE.score"),
>   list("Behavior ~ VES + Inauthenticity",        beh.long,    "behavior ~ VE.score + cringe.score_fake",   "cringe.score_fake",    "behavior ~ VE.score")
> )
> re.part <- " + (1 | part.num)"
> re.stim <- " + (1 | part.num) + (1 | stim.id)"
> sens.table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sens.specs, function(s) {
>   data <- s[[2]]
>   m.part <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(s[[3]], re.part)), data)
>   m.stim <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(s[[3]], re.stim)), data)
>   e.part <- fx(m.part$model, s[[4]])
>   e.stim <- fx(m.stim$model, s[[4]])
>   lrt.part <- lrt.stim <- NULL
>   if (!is.na(s[[5]])) {
>     lrt.part <- lrt(lmer(as.formula(paste0(s[[5]], re.part)), data = data), m.part$model)
>     lrt.stim <- lrt(lmer(as.formula(paste0(s[[5]], re.stim)), data = data), m.stim$model)
>   }
>   data.frame(
>     model           = s[[1]],
>     term            = s[[4]],
>     B.part          = round(e.part$B, 2),  SE.part = round(e.part$SE, 2),  p.part = signif(e.part$p, 3),
>     B.stim          = round(e.stim$B, 2),  SE.stim = round(e.stim$SE, 2),  p.stim = signif(e.stim$p, 3),
>     LRT.part        = if (is.null(lrt.part)) NA else round(lrt.part$chisq, 2),
>     LRT.stim        = if (is.null(lrt.stim)) NA else round(lrt.stim$chisq, 2),
>     status.stim     = m.stim$status,
>     same.conclusion = (e.part$p < .05) == (e.stim$p < .05)
>   )
> }))

> fit_flag <- function(formula, data) {
>   warns <- character(0)
>   m <- withCallingHandlers(
>     lmer(formula, data = data),
>     warning = function(w) { warns <<- c(warns, conditionMessage(w)); invokeRestart("muffleWarning") })
>   status <- if (length(warns) > 0) "convergence warning" else if (isSingular(m)) "singular fit" else "converged"
>   list(model = m, status = status)
> }
> fx_pair <- function(analysis, effect, formula, data, term, stim) {
>   part <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(formula, " + (1 | part.num)")), data)
>   both <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(formula, " + (1 | part.num) + (1 | ", stim, ")")), data)
>   a <- fx(part$model, term); b <- fx(both$model, term)
>   data.frame(analysis, effect, B.part = a$B, SE.part = a$SE, p.part = a$p,
>              B.stim = b$B, SE.stim = b$SE, df.stim = b$df, p.stim = b$p, status.stim = both$status)
> }
> emm_pair <- function(analysis, formula, data, slope = FALSE) {
>   part <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(formula, " + (1 | part.num)")), data)
>   both <- fit_flag(as.formula(paste0(formula, " + (1 | part.num) + (1 | stimulus)")), data)
>   get <- function(m) {
>     # Satterthwaite df (Kenward-Roger is too memory-intensive for 8,100 rows)
>     s <- if (slope) summary(test(emtrends(m, ~ pun.type, var = "cringe.score.z",
>                                           lmer.df = "satterthwaite"), adjust = "holm"))
>          else summary(pairs(emmeans(m, ~ cond | pun.type, lmer.df = "satterthwaite"), reverse = TRUE),
>                       by = NULL, adjust = "holm")
>     data.frame(effect = as.character(s$pun.type), B = s[[if (slope) "cringe.score.z.trend" else "estimate"]],
>                SE = s$SE, df = s$df, p = s$p.value)
>   }
>   a <- get(part$model); b <- get(both$model)
>   data.frame(analysis, effect = a$effect, B.part = a$B, SE.part = a$SE, p.part = a$p,
>              B.stim = b$B, SE.stim = b$SE, df.stim = b$df, p.stim = b$p, status.stim = both$status)
> }

  <tfoot>
    <tr class="gt_sourcenotes">
      <td class="gt_sourcenote" colspan="8"><span class='gt_from_md'><em>Note.</em> <em>N</em> = 405. Analysis numbers follow Table 4. The participant-only models are those reported in the main text; the models with crossed random intercepts for participant and vignette were preregistered. Vignette identity was the 10 main vignettes (five per condition) for Analyses 1–3, 5, and 6; the five intent vignettes for Analysis 7; and the three reputation vignettes for Analysis 12. In Analyses 1–3, condition is confounded with vignette set, so the condition effect in the crossed models is estimated from 10 vignettes. Coefficients for condition compare cringe with vicarious embarrassment; Analysis 7 compares intentional with accidental, and Analysis 12 compares public with private. Analysis 5 used raw Cringe Scale scores and Analysis 6 standardized scores. Analyses 3 and 6 report simple effects and simple slopes by punishment type, Holm-adjusted across the four types; Analysis 2 <em>p</em> values are Benjamini–Hochberg adjusted across the eight outcomes; all other <em>p</em> values are unadjusted. <em>df</em> were estimated with the Satterthwaite method. Bold rows are effects that were significant (<em>p</em> &lt; .05) in one model but not the other. All models with both random intercepts converged without singular fits.</span></td>
    </tr>
  </tfoot>

> if (file.exists("Tables/table_s5_stimulus_sensitivity.docx")) file.remove("Tables/table_s5_stimulus_sensitivity.docx")
> gtsave(table.sens, "Tables/table_s5_stimulus_sensitivity.docx")
> cringe.only <- cringe.s5 |>
>   filter(cond == "cringe") |>
>   mutate(vign45      = as.numeric(scenario %in% c(4, 5)),        # vignettes 4-5 vs. 1-3
>          scenario.f  = factor(scenario),
>          norm.viol.w = norm.viol - ave(norm.viol, part.num))
> vign.means <- cringe.only |>
>   group_by(scenario) |>
>   summarise(moral = mean(moral), punish = mean(punish), norm.viol = mean(norm.viol),
>             n = n(), .groups = "drop")
> vign.means

[1] 0.956611
> cor(vign.means$punish, vign.means$norm.viol)
[1] 0.9630816
> sev.models <- lapply(c(moral = "moral", punish = "punish"), function(dv) list(
>   before = lmer(as.formula(paste(dv, "~ vign45 + (1 | part.num)")), data = cringe.only),
>   after  = lmer(as.formula(paste(dv, "~ vign45 + norm.viol.w + (1 | part.num)")), data = cringe.only)))
> do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sev.models), function(dv) {
>   b0 <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$before, "vign45"); b1 <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$after, "vign45")
>   nv <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$after, "norm.viol.w")
>   data.frame(DV = dv, B.before = b0$B, SE.before = b0$SE, B.after = b1$B, SE.after = b1$SE,
>              p.after = b1$p, pct.explained = round(100 * (1 - b1$B / b0$B)),
>              B.norm.viol = nv$B, SE.norm.viol = nv$SE)
> }))
      DV B.before SE.before   B.after SE.after      p.after pct.explained
1  moral 38.49917  1.584848 16.631101 1.837321 1.047943e-18            57

  B.norm.viol SE.norm.viol

2   0.2847938   0.02579540
> apa.p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", sub("^0", "", sprintf("%.3f", p)))
> ns.df <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(sev.models), function(dv) {
>   b0 <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$before, "vign45")
>   b1 <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$after,  "vign45")
>   nv <- fx(sev.models[[dv]]$after,  "norm.viol.w")
>   data.frame(
>     outcome = ifelse(dv == "moral", "Moral wrongness", "Punishment"),
>     B.0  = b0$B, SE.0  = b0$SE, p.0  = apa.p(b0$p),
>     B.1  = b1$B, SE.1  = b1$SE, p.1  = apa.p(b1$p),
>     pct  = 100 * (1 - b1$B / b0$B),
>     B.nv = nv$B, SE.nv = nv$SE, p.nv = apa.p(nv$p)
>   )
> }))
> n.part <- length(unique(cringe.only$part.num))
> n.rows <- nrow(cringe.only)
> r.moral  <- cor(vign.means$moral,  vign.means$norm.viol)
> r.punish <- cor(vign.means$punish, vign.means$norm.viol)

>   tab_source_note(md(sprintf(paste0(
>     "*Note.* *N* = %d participants in the cringe condition (%s ratings). This analysis was exploratory. ",
>     "Linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for participant; *df* were estimated with the ",
>     "Satterthwaite method. Vignettes 4–5 vs. 1–3 is a dummy code (1 = Vignette 4 or 5). Model 2 adds ",
>     "perceived norm violation, person-mean centered so that it reflects how much more a participant saw a ",

>     n.part, format(n.rows, big.mark = ","),

Linear mixed-effects models with a random intercept for participant; <em>df</em> were estimated with the Satterthwaite method. Vignettes 4–5 vs. 1–3 is a dummy code (1 = Vignette 4 or 5). Model 2 adds perceived norm violation, person-mean centered so that it reflects how much more a participant saw a vignette as violating norms than their own average. % explained = the percentage of the Model 1 difference accounted for by norm violation, 100 × (1 − <em>B</em> Model 2 / <em>B</em> Model 1). Across the five vignette means, norm violation correlated <em>r</em> = .96 with moral wrongness and <em>r</em> = .96 with punishment.</span></td>

research_questions Our objectives in this study are three-fold:
1. Validate the psychometric properties of our cringe sensitivity scale.
2. Confirm that our selected cringe stimuli are indeed perceived as cringey.
3. Determine whether cringe sensitivity scale score is associated with individual cringe assessments.

H1: A confirmatory factor analysis will find evidence for our 2-factor scale of trait-cringe.
To address objective 1, we will conduct a Confirmatory Factor Analysis of our 20-item cringe sensitivity scale specifying the following factor structure: items 1-12 load onto factor 1 (general cringe) and items 13-20 will load onto factor 2 (fakeness-inauthenticity). We hypothesize that our model-implied covariance matrix Σ(θ) will be equal to the observed covariance matrix Σ. The alternative hypothesis is that the model implied covariance matrix is not equal to the observed covariance matrix. In this case, we do not want to reject the null hypothesis.

H0 : Σ(θ) = Σ
H1 : Σ(θ)̸ = Σ

Additionally, we expect that our two correlated factor model will fit the data better than a second- order two-factor model

H2: Cringe stimuli will be rated as more cringey than the neutral stimuli.
To address objective 2, we will conduct a Randomized Controlled Trial in which treatment group participants will receive cringey stimuli, and control group participants will receive neutral stimuli. We hypothesize that our cringe manipulation will result in a statistically significant average treatment effect such that stimuli in our cringe condition will be rated as higher in cringe than the neutral condition at α = 0.05.

H3: Scores on our trait-cringe scale will predict cringe perceptions in the cringe vignettes and videos.
To address objective 3, we will pool all participants and estimate an association between cringe sensitivity scale scores and cringe assessments. We hypothesize a statistically significant association between trait cringe sensitivity and cringe assessments at α = 0.05. 		Our objectives in this study are three-fold:
1. Validate the psychometric properties of the Cringe Sensitivity Scale.
2. Determine whether cringe is a distinct latent construct from vicarious embarrassment.
3. Determine whether cringe is associated with behavioral outcomes and intentions.

Hypothesis 1. A Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) will provide supportive evidence for our 2-
factor Cringe Scale. Specifically, we expect that items 1-12 from the Cringe Scale will load on to factor η1 (general cringe), and that items 13-20 will load on to factor η2 (fakeness/inauthenticity). Further, we hypothesize that our model-implied covariance matrix Σ(Θ) will be equal to the observed covariance matrix Σ. We denote this as:
H0 : Σ(θ) = Σ
H1 : Σ(θ) ≠Σ
In this case, we do not want to reject the null hypothesis.

Hypothesis 2. Discriminant validity testing will provide evidence in support for our hypothesis that cringe and vicarious embarrassment are distinct constructs.

Hypothesis 3a. Cringe scale scores will be significantly associated with donation and
intention behaviors such that higher cringe scores will be associated with lower donations and intentions of engaging in the relevant behavior.

Hypothesis 3b. The video treatment condition (cringe, neutral) will be significantly associated with donation and intention behaviors such that donations and behavioral intentions will be lower in the cringe condition than the control condition.

1. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as more cringe than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes and will rate the vicariously embarrassing vignettes as more vicariously embarrassing than the cringe vignettes.
2. Participants will rate the cringe vignettes as lower in empathy, norm awareness, prosocial motivation, and attention seeking, but higher in norm violation, punishment, moral wrongness, and intent, than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes.

10. Reported perceptions of cringe will be higher when experienced publicly in front of others than when experienced privately. 		Our objectives in this study are three-fold:
1. Validate the psychometric properties of the Cringe Sensitivity Scale.
2. Determine whether cringe is a distinct latent construct from vicarious embarrassment.
3. Determine whether cringe is associated with behavioral outcomes and intentions.

Hypothesis 1. A Confirmatory Factor Analysis (CFA) will provide supportive evidence for our 2-
factor Cringe Scale. Specifically, we expect that items 1-12 from the Cringe Scale will load on to factor η1 (general cringe), and that items 13-20 will load on to factor η2 (fakeness/inauthenticity). Further, we hypothesize that our model-implied covariance matrix Σ(Θ) will be equal to the observed covariance matrix Σ. We denote this as:
H0 : Σ(θ) = Σ
H1 : Σ(θ) ≠Σ
In this case, we do not want to reject the null hypothesis.

Hypothesis 2. Discriminant validity testing will provide evidence in support for our hypothesis that cringe and vicarious embarrassment are distinct constructs.

Hypothesis 3a. Cringe scale scores will be significantly associated with donation and
intention behaviors such that higher cringe scores will be associated with lower donations and intentions of engaging in the relevant behavior.

Hypothesis 3b. The video treatment condition (cringe, neutral) will be significantly associated with donation and intention behaviors such that donations and behavioral intentions will be lower in the cringe condition than the control condition.

5. Cringe scale scores will positively predict appropriateness ratings of the punishment responses.

6. Intent will mediate the relationship between emotion condition (cringe, vicarious embarrassment) and moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions.
7. Moral wrongness judgements and norm violation perceptions will mediate the relationship between intent and prosocial motivation and punishment ratings.
8. The global model with intent will fit the data better than the model without intent.

study_design_overview Using the online platform Prolific, we will randomly assign participants to the treatment or control group in a between-subject design. Both groups will self-report their agreement with items in our cringe scale. After this, they will read a series of short vignettes, longer vignettes, and watch several short videos. The treatment group’s stimuli are intended to be cringey, while the control group’s stimuli are intended to be non-cringey. Specific details about the stimuli will be presented in the Appendix.

The order in which stimuli will be presented will be randomized within each condition. Our intended sample size is n = 300, with n = 150 assigned to each group. We will deliberately oversample by 10 to account for attrition and failed attention checks. This study is single-blind, as the participants will not know to which condition they were assigned, but we will know this information. 		Participants will self-report their agreement with our 20-item Cringe Scale and with an 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (Uysal et al., 2014). The order of which scale is presented first will be randomized within-participants. Participants will then read five short and three long cringe vignettes. They will provide a cringe assessment after each vignette on a sliding scale of 0-100. The order of stimuli will be randomized across participants.

Participants will then be randomly assigned to a treatment group (Cringe) or control group (Control) between-subjects. The Cringe group will watch five short videos which induce cringe (hereafter, “cringe videos”). The Control group will watch five short neutral videos which should not induce cringe (“control videos”). After each video, participants in each condition will be asked to donate a portion of a $1 bonus to the organization that produced the video or they will be asked about their intention to perform an action related to the video.

Participants will then answer several demographic questions, following which the study will end. 		Participants will be randomly assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment condition between-subjects, an intent or accidental behavior condition between-subjects, and a public or private reputation condition between-subjects. Participants will see five cringe or vicariously embarrassing scenarios depending on their experimental condition and will answer a series of measures for each (see Behavior dimension ratings in Measures). After participants receive those five behaviors, they will generate their own example of cringe or vicarious embarrassment (depending on their condition assignment) and answer the same set of measures. Participants will then see five more behaviors that vary in their intent (intentional or accidental) and will rate their cringe and vicarious embarrassment perceptions for each. Next, participants will receive the reputation manipulation in which they will read three scenarios depicting social transgressions that vary in whether they occur publicly or privately. Participants will report their cringe perceptions for each scenario. Lastly, participants will answer several demographic questions, following which the study will end. randomization Participants will be randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral experimental condition in a between-subject design. Participants will receive all three types of cringe stimuli (short scenarios, long vignettes, and videos) in a randomized order within-subjects. Randomization will be performed using Qualtrics’ randomizer. measured_variables Cringe sensitivity scale Items:
The following items will be evaluated on an agreement scale ranging from “1 - Completely Disagree” to
“7-Completely Agree”. The variable names are in parentheses and emboldened.
1. I fidget or tense up when I watch something embarrassing happen. (physical1)
2. I feel my cheeks heat up when something embarrassing happens to others around me. (physical2)
3. I get nervous when I see someone else in an awkward or uncomfortable situation. (physical3)
4. I get a tight feeling in my chest when I witness embarrassing moments. (physical4)
5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd. (ve1)
6. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation. (ve2)
7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes. (ve3)
8. If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me. (ve4)
9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations. (norm1)
10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable. (norm2)
11. I get anxious when I’m around people who don’t seem to understand or care about social rules. (norm3)
12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way. (norm4)
13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are. (fake1)
14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations. (fake2)
15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others. (fake3)
16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen. (fake4)
17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable. (fake5)
18. It’s embarrassing when someone’s confidence comes across as staged or forced. (fake6)
19. It’s embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation. (fake7)
20. I feel uneasy when someone’s behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished. (fake8)

Cringe Assessment:
In response to the cringe stimuli (i.e. short scenarios, long vignettes, videos), participants will be given the following direction: “Please rate the extent to which you perceive each scenario/video as ‘cringe’.” They will then use a 100 point sliding scale with text anchors at each pole reading “Not cringe at all” to “Extremely cringe.”

Demographics:
We will ask questions about age, gender, race, education, household income, english fluency, and primary language. We will also ask participants what they thought the study was about and whether they had seen the videos before. 		1. Cringe scale items
The following items will be evaluated on a Likert scale ranging from “1 - Completely Disagree” to
“7-Completely Agree”. The variable names are in parentheses.
1. I fidget or tense up when I watch something embarrassing happen. (physical1)
2. I feel my cheeks heat up when something embarrassing happens to others around me. (physical2)
3. I get nervous when I see someone else in an awkward or uncomfortable situation. (physical3)
4. I get a tight feeling in my chest when I witness embarrassing moments. (physical4)
5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd. (ve1)
6. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation. (ve2)
7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes. (ve3)
8. If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me. (ve4)
9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations. (norm1)
10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable. (norm2)
11. I get anxious when I’m around people who don’t seem to understand or care about social rules. (norm3)
12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way. (norm4)
13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are. (fake1)
14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations. (fake2)
15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others. (fake3)
16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen. (fake4)
17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable. (fake5)
18. It’s embarrassing when someone’s confidence comes across as staged or forced. (fake6)
19. It’s embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation. (fake7)
20. I feel uneasy when someone’s behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished. (fake8)

2. Vicarious Embarrassment Scale
An 8-item scale from Uysal et al., 2014. All item responses presented on 7-point Likert scale anchored from “1 - Completely disagree” to “7 - Completely agree.”
1. I worry about others making a fool out of themselves. (ves1)
2. I’m afraid of someone saying stupid things and being mortified in public. (ves2)
3. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation. (ves3)
4. I get embarrassed by people becoming an object of ridicule. (ves4)
5. When fictional characters (e.g. novel, film, theater) embarrass themselves, I feel embarrassed, too. (ves5)
6. It makes me feel uncomfortable when I see someone disgrace himself/herself in public. (ves6)
7. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd. (ves7)
8. I feel embarrassed when I see someone disgracing himself/herself. (ves8)

3. State cringe ratings
In response to the five short and three long cringe vignettes, participants will be given the following direction: “Please rate the extent to which you perceive each scenario as ‘cringey’. They will then use a 0-100pt sliding scale anchored from “0 - Not cringe at all” to “100 - Extremely cringe.”

4. Behavioral Measures
4a. Incentivized donation task: participants will receive $1 and will make a dictator game decision about how much of that $1 to allocate to a charity and how much to keep for themselves using a sliding scale.
4b. Intention/likelihood: Participants will report their likelihood of engaging in the target behavior.
All responses will be on a sliding scale anchored from ”0 - Much less likely” to ”100 - Much more likely.” These target behaviors include:
1. Are you more or less likely to speak to your family and friends about mental health after watching this video?
2. Are you more or less likely to purchase food from McDonalds after watching the video?
3. Are you more or less likely to donate to the Truth Initiative after watching the video?
Additionally, participants will also be provided a link to donate to the Truth Initiative, and we will monitor the click rates as an outcome variable.

5. Demographics and covariates
In addition to basic demographic questions (age, gender, race, education, political & party affiliation, income) we will ask questions assessing whether participants had seen the videos before, their cringe perceptions of those videos, their use of social media, and enjoyment of cringe comedy. Participants will also answer a series of covariate items assessing personal experience with the behaviors from the videos. Lastly, participants will self-report their cringe sensitivity (“On a scale of 1 - 100, how sensitive are you to cringey situations?”). 		Vignette intensity ratings: Self-report ratings on 100pt sliding scale measuring the following constructs.
Cringe: How much cringe would you feel observing this situation?
Vicarious embarrassment: How much second-hand embarrassment would you feel observing this situation?

Behavior dimension ratings: Delf-report ratings on 100pt sliding scale measuring the following constructs.
Affective empathy: To what extent do you feel the same emotions that someone in this scenario is feeling?
Moral wrongness: How morally wrong is the act described in this scenario?
Norm awareness: Do you think the person in this scenario was aware that they violated a social norm or acted inappropriately?
Norm violation: To what extent do you think that the person in this scenario violated a social norm or social convention?
Attention seeking: To what extent do you think that the person in this scenario was trying to get attention or impress others?
Intent: How intentional was the behavior in this scenario?
Punishment: In your opinion, should the person in this scenario be punished by others?
Punish response: Please rate how appropriate each of the following behaviors would be in response to the person’s actions described in this scenario. [nothing, gossip, social exclusion, verbal confrontation]
Prosocial motivation: Imagine that you later saw the person in this scenario drop a handful of change. How likely would you be to stop and help them pick it up?

Prosocial motivation: Imagine that you later saw the person in this scenario drop a handful of change. How likely would you be to stop and help them pick it up?

The Cringe Scale: A 20-item Cringe Scale with all item responses presented on a 7-point-Likert scale anchored from “1-Complete disagree” to “7-Completely agree.”
1. I fidget or tense up when I watch something embarrassing happen.
2. I feel my cheeks heat up when something embarrassing happens to others around me.
3. I get nervous when I see someone else in an awkward or uncomfortable situation.
4. I get a tight feeling in my chest when I witness embarrassing moments.
5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd.
6. I get embarrassed by others’ public humiliation.
7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes.
8 If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me.
9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations.
10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable.
11. I get anxious when I’m around people who don’t seem to understand or care about social rules.
12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way.
13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are.
14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations.
15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others.
16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen.
17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable.
18. It’s embarrassing when someone’s confidence comes across as staged or forced.
19. It’s embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation.
20. I feel uneasy when someone’s behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished.
indices Cringe sensitivity scale scores will be calculated by averaging responses across the 20 items of the scale, creating one score for each individual’s cringe sensitivity. Technically, we will be creating scale scores, rather than indices. We will take a row mean of individual responses to the 20-item Cringe Scale to create a Cringe Scale score for each individual. We will also take a row mean of the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (Uysal et al., 2014) to create a Vicarious Embarrassment scale score for each individual. missing_data_handling Following planned exclusions, if the proportion of observations having any missing data is < 3%, we will perform complete case analysis. In the unlikely event that this threshold is ≥ 3%, then we will perform a sensitivity analysis using multiple imputations through chained equations with the number of imputations M equal to max(5, 100f ), where f is the proportion of observations with any missing data. Following data exclusions, if the proportion of observations having any missing data is < 3%, we will perform complete case analysis. In the event that this threshold is ≥ 3%, then we will perform a sensitivity analysis using multiple imputations through chained equations with the number of imputations M equal to max(5, 100f), where f is the proportion of observations with any missing data (following Harrell, 2025). For any item-level missing data from participants who do not fail our attention check, we will conduct sensitivity analyses with complete data generated using multiple imputation through chained equations (MICE). Based on the recommendations of Harrell (n.d.), if the proportion of observations having any data missing is < 3%, we will employ complete case analysis. If the proportion of observations with missing data is ≥ 3%, we may use the MICE approach as a sensitivity analysis, with the number of imputations equal to max(5, 100f) where f is the proportion of observations with any missing data. exploratory_analyses We may run additional regression models as exploratory analyses to determine if the modality of the stimulus (i.e. short vignette, long vignette, video) modify the association between treatment condition and cringe assessment. Similar other models may be fit to explore potential interaction effects between variables. We may also perform additional regression by demographic subgroups to determine if there are any subgroup-specific effects. Since we do not have a priori hypotheses for these models, they will be clearly labelled as exploratory in the final write-up of the results.
