Full text

Abstract

All of our code, materials, and data are publicly available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/t4dex/?view_only=9bb809879ee7418bb9c1003685523d17). Draft version 2.0, 11/4/26. This paper has not been peer reviewed.

Why We Cringe: Understanding the Function of Cringe in Social Cognition

Cringe-a term used to describe situations perceived as intensely embarrassing, awkward, or just generally discomforting-is ubiquitous in modern culture and social life. It is used without elaboration on the pages of the New York Times (McNicholas, 2025), graduation commencement speeches (Swift, 2022), social media platforms (Reddit, 2026), and throughout popular media. Yet, despite its growing usage and ubiquity in everyday life, we currently understand very little about cringe as an emotional state or trait. Although cringe is commonly used as an evaluative label for socially inept behavior ("he is so cringe"), it is more than a descriptor-it exhibits features that most emotion theorists view as constituting emotion, such as reliable antecedents, appraisal processes, and action tendencies (Ekman, 1992 (Ekman, , 2016;; Keltner & Buswell, 1997). Nor is cringe a new concept; while its use has surged in recent years, the underlying affective state we call cringe likely predates the contemporary usage of the term (e.g., cringeworthy dates back to the 1970s; Oxford English Dictionary, n.d.). Cringe warrants greater scientific attention because of its growing role in social life. It has become a monetized media commodity (Mayer et al., 2021), shapes how audiences respond to persuasive messaging (Escoe et al., 2025), and is frequently used to label and shame non-conforming individuals, particularly on social media. Cringe may also contribute to social-developmental difficulties among young people: the fear of being labeled cringe, and the shame associated with it, has been linked to social anxiety (Mzizi, 2025; The Learning Network, 2025), and in a recent Yahoo/YouGov poll, more than half of adult Gen Z respondents reported that fear of seeming cringe had kept them from expressing themselves online and from opening up emotionally (Weekman, 2026).

While academic work on cringe remains sparse, the way the term is colloquially used suggests that it is likely a social emotion, given its close connection to social interaction and expectations, and thus differs from basic emotions such as fear, sadness, or disgust (Ekman, 1992; Izard, 1992). Moreover, cringe is perhaps best conceptualized as a "self-conscious emotion"-a category of social emotions that relate to our sense of self, arise from our awareness of how others perceive us, and are highly sensitive to social context in their expression and intensity (Hareli & Parkinson, 2008; Thomas et al., 2018; Tracy et al., 2009). Self-conscious emotions such as shame, embarrassment, and guilt play important roles in maintaining and repairing social relationships following social transgressions that damage the transgressor's reputation, as well as motivating individuals to behave in moral, socially appropriate ways (Thomas et al., 2018; Tracy et al., 2009; Tracy & Robins, 2004). This emphasis on adaptive functions underlies the form-function approach to studying emotions which holds that an emotion's form (e.g., its features and characteristics) is shaped by its function, the adaptive problem it evolved to solve (Cosmides & Tooby, 2000; Nesse, 1990; Sznycer, 2019). In this view, self-conscious emotions are adaptations for navigating social life: following a transgression, they serve a "recalibration" function that bolsters others' evaluations of the transgressor and maintains cooperative relationships (Sznycer, 2019; Sznycer et al., 2021; Thomas et al., 2018). We draw on the form-function approach here to conceptualize cringe in relation to other self-conscious social emotions. 1Specifically, we propose that cringe may have a function in human social cognition, akin to but distinct from embarrassment or shame, in underlying social norm conformity and enforcement. Social norms are the tacit, unwritten rules that govern and constrain human behavior (Bicchieri, 2016; Legros & Cislaghi, 2020) and play a crucial role in underlying collective action and cooperation in groups (Fehr & Fischbacher, 2004; Ostrom, 2000). Recent work finds that norm cognition and enforcement are proximately motivated by social emotions such as shame and embarrassment (Packard & Schultz, 2023; Schaumberg & Skowronek, 2022; Thomas et al., 2018). For example, a growing literature demonstrates the importance of righteous anger and moral outrage in underlying norm enforcement-the anger we feel witnessing a freerider violate fairness norms motivates us to punish them, even when personally costly (Ginther et al., 2022; Jordan & Rand, 2020). We hypothesize that, like moral outrage, cringe may serve an important function underlying norm compliance and enforcement-but unlike outrage, does so specifically for conventional norm violations (e.g., how we dress, behave in public, etc. ;

Rakoczy & Schmidt, 2013), rather than more serious moral violations.

Does Cringe Differ from Vicarious Embarrassment in Its Elicitation and Social Function?

Cringe is closely related to vicarious embarrassment (or secondhand embarrassment), the feeling of embarrassment derived from witnessing someone else embarrass themselves (Krach et al., 2011; Uysal et al., 2014; Ziegler et al., 2022). Cringe, like vicarious embarrassment, is best conceptualized as a "secondhand emotion" felt vicariously through others when witnessing their transgression (regardless of whether the target is outwardly embarrassed or not). Moreover, both cringe and vicarious embarrassment are experienced in response to witnessing faux pas, social ineptitude, or low-stakes norm violations, and both can elicit unconscious physiological and behavioral responses such as blushing or gaze avoidance (Thorstenson et al., 2020). Lastly, cringe and vicarious embarrassment are both generally associated with a sense of discomfort and displeasure from witnessing a transgression, though somewhat paradoxically both can also be humorous, as demonstrated by the popularity of "cringe comedy" (Mayer et al., 2021).

Like most social emotions, including vicarious embarrassment, we propose that cringe can be measured as both a temporary fleeting state and as a stable dispositional trait. We define state cringe as a transient, affective response to a specific perceived norm-violating situation or behavior, and cringe perceptions as evaluations of an individual or situation as state cringeinducing. We define trait cringe as a stable individual difference in the tendency to react with feelings of awkwardness, unpleasantness, or avoidance in response to others' norm violations.

Consequently, we predict that there will be inter-individual differences in trait cringe sensitivity such that some individuals have a greater tendency to perceive and experience cringe compared to others. Moreover, as with many emotions, state and trait cringe are likely associated (O'Malley & Gillette, 1984), such that high trait cringe is related to stronger feelings of temporary state cringe and perceptions of others as cringeworthy.

Despite their similarities, there are several important differences between vicarious embarrassment and cringe which suggest they may not be entirely overlapping constructs. While vicarious embarrassment is elicited by observing normative transgressions, general ineptitude, or maladroitness, cringe is likely felt almost exclusively when witnessing normative transgressions.

Another potential key distinction between cringe and vicarious embarrassment concerns the perceived motivation of the transgressor-that is, why they transgressed. Specifically, transgressors who elicit cringe may differ from those that elicit vicarious embarrassment in two key respects. First, while vicarious embarrassment is often the result of unintentional actions (e.g., tripping in front of an attractive person, calling your teacher or boss "mom"), cringe is more likely to be elicited in response to intentional actions (e.g., trying to use slang to appear hip, wearing white to a wedding when you are not the bride). Second, while embarrassment is associated with feelings of empathy, sympathy, or pity for the embarrassing individual (Krach et al., 2011; Miller, 1987; Stocks et al., 2011), the same is not true for cringe. We propose that when people experience cringe, they are relatively less inclined to empathize with or help the transgressor and more motivated to distance themselves from them (whether physically or reputationally).

In one of the only empirical studies of cringe, Escoe et al. (2025) defined cringe as a form of vicarious embarrassment in which an actor makes an awkward attempt at forming a positive impression in a way that is inexcusable. Excusability refers to the observer's appraisal of the actor's transgression as forgivable because they are able to take the actor's perspective and understand why they transgressed. In this view, cringe arises when observers fail to take the actor's perspective, resulting in negative attitudes and reduced compassion toward the transgressor. Escoe et al. distinguish cringe from empathetic embarrassment, which occurs when the transgression is excusable and is consequently associated with more positive attitudes and greater compassion toward the transgressor. In this account, sharing cringe content is motivated by downward social comparison that boosts perceptions of one's own social savviness (i.e., the extent to which "the situation makes you feel as though others are not as socially aware as you are"; Escoe et al., 2025, p. 670).

Escoe's account implies that, because cringe arises when observers fail to excuse the actor's behavior, it should be accompanied by less empathy than empathetic embarrassment. Consequently, we measured whether participants experienced differences in empathy and sympathy toward the transgressor between cringe-inducing and vicariously embarrassing scenarios. Additionally, prior work shows that observers' responses depend on why a norm was violated: vicarious embarrassment and compassion tend to be weaker when the violation is intentional, and arousal is stronger when the actor is aware of the violation (Krach et al., 2011; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012). However, this work did not distinguish vicarious embarrassment from cringe, and many of its stimuli resemble what people colloquially call cringe (e.g., "you are in a café: the person next to you is listening to music and singing along loudly"; Müller-Pinzler et al., 2012, p. 76), raising the possibility that intent is precisely what separates cringe from vicarious embarrassment. Because intentional violations are treated as diagnostic of an actor's character in a way that accidental ones are not (Epley & Waytz, 2010; Reeder, 2009), cringe should differentially shape attitudes and behavior toward the transgressor as compared to vicarious embarrassment. Therefore, we measured participants' judgments of the transgressor's actions as intentional as well as their prosocial motivation to help them, their desire to distance themselves from the transgressor, and their willingness to endorse socially sanctioning them.

Present Study

Across five studies (three preregistered) we investigated the characteristics and components of trait and state cringe. We had three main aims in the present work. First, if cringe is a genuine affective state with a dispositional component, we should be able to measure individual differences in it, and those differences should predict how people actually respond to cringe-inducing content. To do this, we developed and validated a novel scale to measure individual differences in trait cringe sensitivity (henceforth Cringe Scale) and tested whether it predicts perceptions of situations as cringe-inducing, influenced behavioral outcomes, and assessed its discriminant and criterion validity (Studies 1-3). Second, to determine whether cringe is a distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment that differs in its effect on social attitudes and behavior, we tested whether cringe is associated with dissociable effects on social evaluation, empathic responses, behavioral outcomes, and attitudes on punishment and social sanctioning as compared to vicarious embarrassment (Studies 3-5). Additionally, to support our hypothesis that attributed intent is what separates cringe from vicarious embarrassment, we tested whether cringe transgressions were perceived as more intentional than vicariously embarrassing transgressions and directly manipulated transgressor intent (Studies 4-5). Third, if cringe functions to motivate norm-enforcement and acts as a social signal, it should be tied to sanctioning and should be stronger when the transgression is public. We test this by investigating whether cringe is more strongly associated with endorsement of punishment and social sanctioning (e.g., gossip) than vicarious embarrassment, and by manipulating whether hypothetical transgressions occur in public or private to determine how reputation salience influences cringe perceptions (Studies 5).

If the Cringe Scale reliably captures trait cringe, discriminates it from trait vicarious embarrassment, and predicts cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes, this would provide evidence that cringe sensitivity is a measurable individual difference that shapes how people respond to cringe-inducing situations that is conceptually distinct from vicarious embarrassment at the trait level. Additionally, if cringe is elicited more strongly than vicarious embarrassment by intentional and public transgressions, and is accompanied by distinct inferences and behavioral attitudes towards the transgressor, this would indicate that cringe is a distinct variety of vicarious embarrassment with its own elicitors and social functions. Importantly, these possibilities are not mutually exclusive: cringe may overlap substantially with vicarious embarrassment at the trait level while still differing in its situational elicitors and social-cognitive consequences.

General Method

Overview of Studies

Studies 1-3 developed and validated the Cringe Scale. Study 1 generated candidate items and conducted an exploratory factor analysis (EFA) to determine the factor structure and loadings.

Study 2 confirmed this structure with confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in a representative sample from the US and tested whether it predicted cringe perceptions. Study 3 replicated the CFA, assessed the scale's discriminant validity from trait vicarious embarrassment, and tested whether it predicted cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes beyond vicarious embarrassment. Studies 4 and 5 examined the appraisals and social inferences that functionally distinguish cringe from vicarious embarrassment, with Study 5 manipulating the transgressor's intent and whether the transgression occurred in public or private. We describe the method for each study in turn below (see Table 1 for a summary of independent and dependent measures across studies).

Transparency and Openness

We adhere to the Journal Article Reporting Standards (Appelbaum et al., 2018) and report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, and all measures in the studies (see Table 1 for a summary of independent and dependent measures across studies). The study designs and analysis plans for three of our five studies (Studies 2, 3, & 5) were preregistered in advance of data collection; Studies 1 and 4 were not preregistered. All of our analysis code, data, preregistrations, and Supplemental Material, including our study stimuli, scale items, and preregistered analyses, are available on the Open Science Framework (Authors, 2026; https://osf.io/t4dex/?view_only=9bb809879ee7418bb9c1003685523d17). Data were analyzed using R Version 4.4.2 (R Core Team, 2024), and with the packages lavaan (Rosseel, 2012), lme4 (Bates et al., 2015), emmeans (Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026), and dplyr (Wickham et al., 2026). 5. I feel embarrassed if someone makes a mistake in front of a crowd.

6. I get embarrassed by others' public humiliation.

7. I tend to anticipate and worry about others making social mistakes.

8. If I witness someone making a social blunder, I feel just as embarrassed as if it happened to me. 9. I feel physically uncomfortable when someone acts out of place or inappropriately in social situations.

10. When people dress or behave in ways that are inappropriate for the occasion, it makes me feel uncomfortable.

11. I get anxious when I'm around people who don't seem to understand or care about social rules.

12. I feel stressed when someone behaves in a socially awkward or out-of-sync way.

13. I feel embarrassed for people who try too hard to appear cooler or more interesting than they actually are.

14. I feel awkward when I see people putting on a fake persona in social situations.

15. I feel uncomfortable watching people try too hard to impress others.

16. When someone is being disingenuous in a conversation, I find it difficult to watch or listen.

17. Seeing someone imitate a trend or behavior just to be part of the crowd makes me uncomfortable.

18. It's embarrassing when someone's confidence comes across as staged or forced.

19. It's embarrassing watching someone seek social approval or validation. 20. I feel uneasy when someone's behavior feels rehearsed or overly polished.

Study 1 Method

Participants

We sampled N = 193 participants (64.8% female), aged 18-75 (MAge = 38.2) from Prolific. Participants were compensated $1.40 for participating in a 7-min survey. We conducted an a priori power calculation using the semPower package (Moshagen & Bader, 2024) in R to determine the number of participants needed to reject a model based on a root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) of 0.05, 169 degrees of freedom, 90% power, and an alpha of 0.05 (Jobst et al., 2023). The analysis suggested a minimum sample of 148 observations. We consequently oversampled to account for potential attrition due to failed attention checks or incomplete submissions.

Design and Procedure

Participants provided informed consent and were given instructions for the task.

Participants then received 80 short items detailing different behaviors (e.g., "I blush when I see something awkward happening") and indicated their agreement with each on a 7-point Likert scale anchored from "1 -Completely disagree" to "7 -Completely agree". The items were drafted by the authors based on a review of existing literature to measure the four initially hypothesized subfactors of cringe: vicarious embarrassmentfoot_1 , physiological reactivity, norm sensitivity, and fakeness-inauthenticity. Participants answered 20 items for each domain as well as an attention check measure ("if you're paying attention, select 2"). Because we hypothesized that cringe is a variety of vicarious embarrassment elicited by distinct triggers, these domains were intended to capture both general vicarious embarrassment (vicarious embarrassment, physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity) and sensitivity to inauthenticity, that is, effortful, insincere, image-motivated self-presentation.

Analysis

We first tested for the suitability of factor analysis using Bartlett's test of sphericity and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin criterion. To determine the number of factors to extract, we examined eigenvalues from principal axis factoring alongside a scree plot. We then conducted an exploratory factor analysis on the 80-items using maximum likelihood estimation with Promax rotation, as we expected the factors to be correlated. Relatedly, we computed the total variance explained by the factors by summing item communalities divided by the number of total items (Revelle, 2026). After extraction and rotation, items were evaluated based on statistical and conceptual criteria. We used a factor loading cutoff of 0.6, indicating a very strong loading to the latent factor, to select the final scale items.

Results

Bartlett's test of sphericity was significant (χ²(3160) = 11034.65, p < .001) and the Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin criterion of sampling adequacy was .914, confirming the suitability of the data for factor analysis. An examination of the eigenvalues and scree plot suggested a two-factor structure: the scree plot revealed a distinct flattening after the second factor and the two factors had eigenvalues of 25.77 and 4.56 from principal axis factoring. After Promax rotation, the two factors explained 25% and 12% of the variance, respectively, and were moderately correlated (r = .58). Together, the two factors explained 38% of the variance in the data. Excluding item factor loadings below 0.6 resulted in 37 items. To avoid redundancy, we removed items that shared similar wording, and to ensure conceptual breadth, selected the remaining items that best captured the intended construct domains. This resulted in 20 final scale items: 12 items capturing the first latent factor of Vicarious Social Anxiety (and which included three of our initially hypothesized domains: vicarious embarrassment, involuntary physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity), and 8 items capturing the second latent factor of Inauthenticity (capturing our fourth hypothesized subcomponent of cringe). See Table 2 for the full Cringe Scale item text.

Discussion

The results of the exploratory factor analysis from Study 1 indicated a two-factor model was most appropriate for capturing individual variability in the Cringe Scale items. Vicarious embarrassment, physiological reactivity, and norm sensitivity loaded onto a single factor, Vicarious Social Anxiety, whereas inauthenticity emerged as a separate factor. We retained both factors because they map onto our account of cringe: Vicarious Social Anxiety captures the vicarious embarrassment that cringe shares with related emotions, whereas Inauthenticity captures sensitivity to the intentional, image-motivated transgressions we hypothesized to be specific to cringe. In the next study, we test this model using confirmatory factor analysis with a new sample.

Study 2

The results of Study 1 allowed us to specify our cringe sensitivity model. In Study 2, we tested this model using confirmatory factor analysis with a new, representative sample of US participants. We also tested for predictive validity of our scale by examining whether individual differences in cringe sensitivity would predict state perceptions of cringe across a series of different stimuli.

Method

Participants

We sampled N = 310 participants (49.7% female), aged 19-85 (MAge = 45.9) from Prolific in a preregistered study with a representative sample from the US population: https://osf.io/ymzqc/overview?view_only=b9463362065e4965b0edd18a728fba9e. Participants received $2.10 in compensation for completing a 12-minute survey. We initially recruited 325 participants but 15 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria (see supplement for specific inclusion criteria). We determined our sample size based on our prior study and established convention with previous online psychometric work (Loustau et al., 2025; Uysal et al., 2014).

Design and Procedure

We selected 20 items from Study 1 based on the results of the exploratory factor analysis (see Table S9 in the supplement). 3 Participants answered these 20 items (12 measuring Vicarious Social Anxiety and 8 measuring Inauthenticity latent factors). After answering the Cringe Scale items, participants were randomly assigned between-subjects to a cringe or neutral scenario condition in which they received 10 short scenarios, 4 vignettes, and 4 short (around 1 minute) videos corresponding to their experimental condition. Participants rated their perceptions of cringe for each stimulus on a 100-point sliding scale anchored from "0 -Not cringe at all" to "100 -Extremely cringe". Both the order of the individual stimuli and of the three stimuli blocks was randomized across participants. Participants then answered several basic demographic questions (age, sex, race, education level, etc.), including items noting whether they had seen the video stimuli previously.

Analysis

We estimated a preregistered two-factor latent model using confirmatory factor analysis with maximum likelihood in which items 1-12 would load onto factor one-Vicarious Social Anxiety-and that items 13-20 would load onto factor two-Inauthenticity. We then conducted a series of planned linear regression models. To determine whether the cringe condition predicted cringe perceptions, we ran a multilevel regression model predicting cringe perceptions by condition (neutral, cringe), controlling for the random effect of participant ID. To test whether individual differences in cringe sensitivity influence perceptions of a situation as cringeworthy, we ran a multilevel regression model predicting cringe perceptions by average Cringe Scale score across the 20-items. To determine whether the type of stimuli influenced cringe perceptions, we ran two exploratory multilevel regression models with cringe perceptions as the response term, one including the interaction of scenario condition and stimuli modality as a predictor, and another with the interaction of Cringe Scale score and stimuli modality as a predictor (see Table S10 in the supplement). We also conducted three exploratory multilevel regression models examining the effect of scenario condition on cringe perceptions for each stimuli type separately (short scenarios, long vignettes, videos). Lastly, we ran two exploratory multilevel regression models predicting cringe perceptions by average Cringe Scale score. The first was identical to the model described above but only included data from the cringe condition, and the second model controlled for the effect of scenario condition. See Table S10 in the supplement for a table listing all our models and estimated effects.

Results

The results of the confirmatory factor analysis largely support our specified factor structure (see Table S8 in the supplement). While the chi-square fit statistic (χ²(169, N = 310) = 481.90, p < .001) indicated that our model did not perfectly reproduce the observed covariance matrix, the incremental model fit indices suggested an acceptable fit to the data: CFI = .925, TLI = .916, RMSEA = .077, 90% CI [.069, .085], SRMR = .051 (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The standardized factor loadings for all items were large and statistically significant (ranging from .60 to .83). The two latent factors-Vicarious Social Anxiety and Inauthenticity-were strongly and positively correlated (r = .795, p < .001). The Cronbach's alpha across all 20-items was 0.95, indicating high internal reliability and suggesting the items were measuring the same underlying construct. See Figure 1 for the Cringe Scale's CFA measurement model and factor loadings.

The stimuli in the cringe condition were perceived as more cringe than those in the neutral stimuli (B = 44.20, SE = 1.70, p < .001). When breaking this down by stimuli type, we found that the short cringe scenarios (B = 47.77, SE = 1.78, p < .001), cringe vignettes (B = 52.67, SE = 2.14, p < .001), and cringe videos (B = 26.78, SE = 2.26, p < .001) were all perceived as more cringe-inducing than the equivalent neutral stimuli. As hypothesized, Cringe Scale score was positively associated with individual cringe assessments of the stimuli across both experimental conditions (B = 4.85, SE = 1.15, p < .001), and this effect was larger when subsetting the data to the cringe condition (B = 6.86, SE = 0.81, p < .001). Moreover, individual differences in cringe sensitivity positively predicted cringe assessments, even when controlling for the effect of scenario condition (B = 4.62, SE = 0.61, p < .001). Additionally, there was no interaction effect between Cringe Scale score and stimuli type (all interaction term p-values > .88; see Table S10), indicating that modality of the stimuli (e.g., video vs vignette) did not influence the relationship between cringe sensitivity and cringe perceptions. factor loadings from Study 2.

Discussion

Study 2's findings provided confirmatory evidence in support of the Cringe Scale's twofactor structure. More generally, these findings suggest that sensitivity to cringe varies systematically across individuals and can be measured using an individual-differences scale.

Moreover, our finding that the Cringe Scale predicted perceptions of a situation as cringeworthy provides evidence of predictive validity for our scale by demonstrating that individual differences in cringe sensitivity are associated with different social perceptions of stimuli as cringe inducing.

Study 3

In Study 3, we further validated the Cringe Scale and tested it's discriminant validity.

Namely, we sought to demonstrate that our scale 1) specifically captures cringe as opposed to vicarious embarrassment, and 2) offers unique predictive validity of cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes above and beyond vicarious embarrassment. Additionally, we investigated the effects of cringe on consumer, public health, and charity messaging, specifically testing whether higher trait cringe was associated with reduced donations and behavioral intentions in response to cringe-inducing videos.

Method

Participants

We sampled N = 307 participants (51.8% female), aged 19-72 (MAge = 38.74) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2q73k/overview?view_only=4ecf65adc28d47ac9ea670175c3bc12b. Participants were compensated $2.50 for participating in a 15-min survey. We initially recruited 328 participants, but 21 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria. We determined our sample size based on our previous studies and established convention with online psychometric work (Loustau et al., 2025; Uysal et al., 2014).

Design and Procedure

Our goal in Study 3 was to replicate the CFA model findings from the previous study and begin to tease apart cringe from vicarious embarrassment. To that end, participants completed our 20-item Cringe Scale from Study 2 as well as the 8-item Vicarious Embarrassment scale (VES; Uysal et al., 2014), which they received in a random order. Participants then answered five short cringe scenarios and three cringe vignettes from the previous study presented in a random order (see Study 3 -Supplementary Materials for stimuli). Participants were then randomly assigned to either a cringe or neutral emotion condition between-subjects and saw five videos corresponding to their assigned condition in a fixed order. They received two videos from nonprofits-the American Red Cross and American Cancer Society-and three videos from other organizations-an Ad Council message on mental health, a McDonald's ad, and the Truth Initiative anti-vaping ad-in that order. Participants completed an incentivized donation task (i.e., a dictator game with the nonprofit as the recipient) after watching each of the nonprofit videos. Specifically, participants received $1 and could divide it between themselves and the nonprofit however they wished in increments of 1 cent. After making their two donation decisions, participants received the other three videos-for each, they were asked to report their intentions of engaging in the target behavior in the video (e.g., "are you more or less likely to purchase food from McDonald's after watching this video"; see Study 3 -Method in the supplement for all intent measures) on a 100-point sliding scale anchored from "0 -Much less likely" to "100 -Much more likely", with a midpoint of "50 -Neither less nor more likely". For the final video from the Truth Initiative's anti-vaping campaign, we also measured whether participants chose to click a provided link to visit the organization's donation page. Participants then reported whether they had seen the videos before and, as a manipulation check, reported their cringe perceptions of each video. To control for factors that might influence donation decisions and behavioral intentions, participants answered a series of questions assessing how often they engage in the target behavior associated with each video (e.g., for the Ad Council video on mental health: "how often do you discuss mental health with family members or friends"). Lastly, participants answered an item assessing how much time they spend on various social media platforms, a one-item cringe sensitivity measure (i.e., "on a scale of 1 -100, how sensitive are you to cringey situations"), as well as a number of demographic questions. See Study 3 -Results in the supplement for the results of the social media and cringe sensitivity analyses.

Analysis

We first replicated our confirmatory factor analysis with a new sample to provide additional evidence of our scale's model fit and internal reliability. To test for discriminant validity between the Cringe Scale and the VES, we used confirmatory factor analysis to compare two models, an unconstrained and a constrained model. The latent factors of Cringe and Vicarious embarrassment were allowed to freely covary with one another in the unconstrained model, whereas the latent correlations were fixed to 0.85 in the constrained model, following the approach of Panzeri et al. (2024). If the unconstrained model demonstrated a latent correlation < 0.85, and had a better model fit than the constrained model-i.e., the difference in CFI between the models is greater than 0.002, and the χ2 difference between the two models is statistically significant (where α = 0.05)-we interpreted this as evidence of discriminant validity.

In order to examine the relationship of trait cringe and vicarious embarrassment on cringe perceptions and behavior, we fit a series of preregistered regression models. All multilevel regression models included participant ID as a random intercept. Specifically, to determine whether the Cringe Scale uniquely predicts cringe perceptions above and beyond the VES, we tested and compared two multilevel regression models-the first predicting cringe perceptions by scores on the vicarious embarrassment scale (Uysal et al., 2014), and the second predicting cringe perceptions by both VES score and Cringe Scale score. We then compared these nested models using a likelihood ratio test to determine whether the model with trait cringe score explains significantly more variance than the model solely including vicarious embarrassment.

To further probe the predictive and discriminant validity of the Cringe Scale, we ran a series of exploratory models predicting cringe perceptions by the VES and each of the Cringe Scale's two latent factors (factor 1: Vicarious Social Anxiety and factor 2: Inauthenticity) and compared each to a nested model including only the VES. Finally, to determine whether the Cringe Scale and VES differed in their ability to predict cringe perceptions, we assessed whether there was a statistically significant difference in the coefficients (α = 0.05) using the approach of Zee (2019). Specifically, we compared regression coefficients using seemingly unrelated regression (SUR) and tested for differences between coefficients using Theil's F test.

We then conducted several regression models predicting behavioral outcomes by Cringe Scale score-we report the results of two models here: the first including incentivized donation decisions as the outcome variable, and the second including behavioral intentions. We report the models individually examining each specific behavioral outcome in the supplement (see Study 3 -Results in the supplement).

To determine whether scenario condition predicted behavioral outcomes, we conducted a series of identical regression models but including scenario condition (neutral, cringe) as the predictor rather than Cringe Scale score. We report the results of the two combined multilevel regression models here (one looking at incentivized donations, the other looking at behavioral intentions) and report the models for each individual behavioral outcome in the supplement.

Next, to determine whether the Cringe Scale predicts behavioral outcomes above and beyond the VES, we compared a multilevel regression model including both Cringe Scale and VES scores as predictors to a nested model including only the VES using a likelihood ratio test, both for overall behavioral outcomes and separately for behavioral intentions and donation decisions. As with cringe perceptions, we also ran exploratory models predicting behavioral outcomes by the VES and each of the Cringe Scale's two latent factors, comparing each to a nested model including only the VES. All multilevel models were refit with an additional random intercept for stimulus identity; all converged and no conclusions changed. Estimates for trait cringe and the VES were virtually identical, and the (non-significant) effects of video condition had larger standard errors because each condition used a different set of five videos.

We report the participant random-intercept models in keeping with our preregistration.

To more clearly test for discriminant validity, we ran a series of exploratory analyses duplicating the CFA and Cringe Scale-VES regression models excluding the two shared items with the VES-we report those results in the supplement; the regression results were consistent with our preregistered models, and the discriminant validity results are summarized below.

Lastly, since the Cringe Scale and VES were highly correlated, we also tested for potential multicollinearity in regression models where both scale scores and their factors were entered as predictors by computing variance inflation factors (VIFs; James et al., 2021). Following common guidance, we treated VIFs > 5 as indicating moderate multicollinearity and VIFs > 10 as indicating severe multicollinearity (James et al., 2021).

Results

The CFA results support the previous findings, suggesting that the hypothesized model provided a reasonably good fit to the data (χ²(169, N = 307) = 434.4, p < .001, CFI = .942, TLI = .934, RMSEA = .072, 90% CI [.063, .080], SRMR = .043). The Cringe Scale was highly correlated with the VES but the strength of the association varied across the two cringe factors:

The latent correlation between Vicarious Social Anxiety and VES was r = 0.919 (95% CI: 0.895, 0.943) and the latent correlation between Inauthenticity and VES was r = 0.756 (95% CI: 0.7, 0.813). The association between the two Cringe Scale latent factors was high and significant, r = 0.87 (p < .001). Following our preregistered criteria (Panzeri et al., 2024), for each Cringe Scale factor we compared a model in which its latent correlation with the VES was freely estimated with one in which that correlation was fixed to .85. Discriminant validity was not supported for either factor. For Vicarious Social Anxiety, the latent correlation exceeded .85 (r = .92, 95% CI [.90, .94]). For Inauthenticity, the latent correlation was below .85 (r = .76, 95% CI [.70, .81]) and constraining it significantly worsened fit (Δχ²(1) = 15.19, p < .001), but the decrease in CFI (.0019) fell just short of the .002 criterion.

In an exploratory analysis excluding the two Cringe Scale items that duplicate VES items verbatim, Inauthenticity met all three criteria (r = .76, 95% CI [.70, .81]; ΔCFI = .0022; Δχ²(1) = 15.19, p < .001), whereas Vicarious Social Anxiety still did not (r = .90, 95% CI [.87, .93]). Because Inauthenticity's correlation with the VES was unchanged (the excluded items loaded on Vicarious Social Anxiety), we treat this result as converging evidence that Inauthenticity is the more distinct factor, not as evidence that its overlap with the VES decreased. Inauthenticity also met the heterotrait-monotrait criterion including both scales as predictors to the model only including VES as a predictor, we found that the model including trait cringe scores explained significantly more variance in cringe perceptions than the model without it (LRT χ² (1) = 9.37, p = .002), suggesting the Cringe Scale offers incremental predictive validity over the VES.

Upon further exploration, we found that this difference was driven by the Inauthenticity subscale: When comparing nested models with VES and each Cringe Scale subscale to models with only VES, we found that the model including Inauthenticity (LRT χ² (1) = 15.03, p < .001), but not Vicarious Social Anxiety (LRT χ² (1) = 2.99, p = .08), explained significantly more variance in cringe perceptions. Multicollinearity was low in the model including VES and the Inauthenticity subscales (VIF = 1.95 for each predictor), and higher for the model including VES and the Vicarious Social Anxiety subscales (VIF = 4.1), though still below the conventional threshold of 5 indicating moderate multicollinearity (James et al., 2021). This suggests that the second Cringe Scale factor-Inauthenticity-specifically provides additional predictive validity of cringe perceptions over the VES. However, when testing whether the Cringe Scale and VES differed in their ability to predict cringe assessments by comparing regression coefficients using seemingly unrelated regression (SUR), we found that a Theil's F test indicated no significant difference between the coefficients (F(1, 590) = 0.10, p = .75), suggesting both scales have equivalent predictive validity for cringe assessments.

The Cringe Scale significantly predicted behavioral outcomes (B = 6.15, SE = 0.94, p < .001), including both behavioral intentions (B = 6.80, SE = 0.99, p < .001) and donation decisions (B = 5.17, SE = 1.46, p < .001), but in the opposite direction of what was predicted; higher trait cringe was positively, rather than negatively, associated with behavioral outcomes.

In an exploratory model, this association did not differ by video condition (Cringe Scale × condition: B = -0.21, SE = 1.90, p = .91), indicating that higher trait cringe was associated with greater donations and intentions regardless of whether participants viewed cringe-inducing or neutral videos. Additionally, there was no effect of emotion condition on overall behavioral outcomes (B = -1.01, SE = 2.55, p = .69), including for behavioral intentions (B = -3.18, SE = 2.68, p = .24), donations (B = 2.25, SE = 3.76, p = .55) and clicking the Truth Initiative donation link (B = 0.29, SE = 0.37, p = .43). The only stimuli for which we observed an effect of emotion condition was for the behavioral intentions to the Ad Council videos on mental health (B = -9.31, SE = 3.19, p = .004), where intentions to discuss mental health with family and friends were lower in the cringe than neutral video.

When comparing the model including both cringe and VES as predictors of behavioral outcomes to a nested model only including the VES, we found that, in contrast to our prediction, the model with cringe did not explain significantly more variance than the model without (LRT χ² (1) = 1.61, p = .21). This held true when separately examining behavioral intentions (LRT χ² (1) = 1.53, p = .22) and donation decisions (LRT χ² (1) = 0.63, p = .43). However, when breaking up the Cringe Scale by its two latent factors, we found that the model including Vicarious Social Anxiety (B = 3.54, SE = 1.73, p = .04) and VES (B = 2.83, SE = 1.65, p = .09), explained significantly more variance in behavioral outcomes than a model with just VES (LRT χ² (1) = 4.20, p = .04), suggesting that the first factor of the Cringe Scale offers unique predictive validity over and above the VES. Because the Vicarious Social Anxiety factor and the VES were highly correlated, multicollinearity was higher in this model (VIF = 4.1 for each predictor) than in the two-factor Cringe Scale models (VIF = 3.4), though still below the conventional cutoff of 5 indicating moderate multicollinearity (James et al., 2021).

Discussion

In Study 3 we replicated the confirmatory factor analysis result for our latent Cringe Scale model a second time, providing additional support for its validity and reliability. We also replicated the effect of the Cringe Scale on vignette cringe perceptions-such that higher trait cringe sensitivity positively predicted cringe perceptions-observed in the previous study. When examining the predictive validity of trait cringe and the closely related emotion of vicarious embarrassment, we found that both the Cringe Scale and the VES predicted state perceptions of cringe across two types of stimuli (short and long vignettes). We also found that the Cringe Scale predicted behavioral outcomes for both behavioral intentions and incentivized donation decisions, indicating that individual differences in cringe sensitivity are associated with real behavioral outcomes.

However, while we had predicted that trait cringe would be associated with lower donations and intentions of engaging in the relevant behavior, we found the opposite: higher trait cringe was positively associated with donations to charity and behavioral intentions. This unexpected pattern of results was primarily driven by the Vicarious Social Anxiety factor which closely parallels vicarious embarrassment (r = .92 with the VES), an emotion characterized by empathic concern (Krach et al., 2011). This suggests that Vicarious Social Anxiety reflects the empathic component of trait cringe shared with vicarious embarrassment and, given that empathy reliably promotes helping and prosocial behavior (Batson, 2011), may explain why higher trait cringe predicted donations to charity and behavioral intentions, regardless of whether the videos were cringe-inducing. By contrast, Inauthenticity, which captures the cringe-specific appraisal of others' behavior as fake, was unrelated to behavior once Vicarious Social Anxiety was controlled. Additionally, we failed to find an effect of the cringe emotion condition on behavioral outcomes with the exception of the Ad Council video on mental health communication. Why did cringe sensitivity, but not cringe condition, predict behavioral outcomes? One possibility is that cringe as a stable, dispositional trait is more closely associated with behavioral outcomes than state cringe as manipulated by the emotion condition. While the cringe stimuli were rated as significantly more cringe than the neutral stimuli, the manipulation may not have been sufficiently strong to translate into measurable differences in behavioral outcomes.

Alternatively, dispositional cringe sensitivity may be more closely associated with behavioral outcomes because it reflects a stable concern for social norms and norm violations. In contrast, the experimental cringe video manipulation may have primarily evoked a transient emotional response without activating the deeper motivational systems associated with norm cognition.

While our findings suggest that the Cringe Scale offered unique predictive validity for social perceptions of cringe above and beyond vicarious embarrassment, we found relatively weak evidence for discriminant validity of the scale on behavior as compared to vicarious embarrassment. That we found scores on the Cringe Scale and the VES were strongly correlated with one another (r = 0.84), and that both significantly predicted cringe perceptions and behavioral outcomes, suggests that cringe and vicarious embarrassment are substantially overlapping constructs. However, when breaking Cringe Scale score into its two latent factors, we found that the Inauthenticity factor predicted cringe perceptions above and beyond VES score, while Vicarious Social Anxiety offered greater explanatory power over vicarious embarrassment for predicting behavioral outcomes. We attribute this discrepancy in predictive validity as reflecting differences in the items for each sub-scale. Specifically, Inauthenticity included items specifically assessing perceived fakeness and inauthenticity which may have contributed to its incremental validity over the VES in cringe perceptions, while Vicarious Social Anxiety closely paralleled the VES but included additional items assessing sensitivity to norm violations which may explain why it offered greater explanatory power over the VES in behavioral outcomes. Additionally, after removing the two shared items with the VES, the Inauthenticity factor demonstrated clear evidence of discriminant validity over the VES, providing additional evidence that Inauthenticity captures a distinct construct from vicarious embarrassment (see Study 3 -Analyses in the supplement).

Together, these findings provide preliminary but inconclusive evidence for the discriminant validity of the Cringe Scale over and above the VES. In the next two studies, we aimed to test whether cringe and vicarious embarrassment differ in their elicitors, the inferences they generate about the transgressor, and their functions in social cognition.

Study 4

Our next set of studies aimed to dissociate cringe from vicarious embarrassment. Because the psychometric analyses indicated that cringe and vicarious embarrassment are largely overlapping constructs, it remains unclear whether cringe meaningfully differs from vicarious embarrassment in its elicitation and influence on social attitudes and behavior. Consequently, in Study 4, participants generated their own examples of cringe and vicarious embarrassment and rated them on several dimensions to identify the main characteristics that differentiate cringe from vicarious embarrassment and their effects on social judgment and evaluation, including those we proposed distinguish the two emotions (empathy, sympathy, perceived intent, and desire for distance from the transgressor).

Method

Participants

We tested N = 200 participants (53.0% female), aged 21-77 (MAge = 41.2) from Prolific.

Participants were compensated $1.85 for participating in a 10-min survey. No participants were excluded from analysis. The sample size was determined based on our previous studies and prior vignette work with online samples (Deutchman et al., 2025; Escoe et al., 2025).

Design and Procedure

Participants were assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment scenario condition between-subjects. Participants were provided with a short, colloquial definition of their condition's emotion (see Study 4 -Supplementary Materials for definition text) and were asked to generate three short example scenarios that best capture that emotion. Next, participants answered a series of measures on 100-point sliding scales for each of their examples. These measures were designed to identify and isolate the factors that may underlie differences between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. Specifically, we assessed emotional valence, sympathy, empathy, self-awareness, intent, social distance, humor, relevance to norms, and intensity of the felt emotion (e.g., cringe or embarrassment depending on condition assignment; see Table 3 for measure text). Participants then answered the same demographic questions from previous studies, as well as a question asking them to report any words or concepts that capture a similar feeling as cringe.

Analysis

We ran nine multilevel regression models predicting each of the dependent measures by condition (cringe, vicarious embarrassment), controlling for the random intercept of participant ID. To control the false discovery rate across multiple comparisons, we used Benjamini-Hochberg corrections (BH; Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995); consequently, all results report BHadjusted p-values.

Results

Participants reported significantly lower levels of empathy (B = -8.27, SE = 3.68, p = .04) and sympathy (B = -11.66, SE = 3.41, p = 0.002) for the transgressor in the cringe scenarios as compared to the vicarious embarrassment scenarios (see Table S2 in the supplement). They also reported that transgressors were less aware that their behavior was perceived by others as cringe in the cringe scenarios than transgressors were aware their behavior was perceived as vicariously embarrassing in the vicarious embarrassment scenarios (B = -10.06, SE = 3.77, p = .015).

Additionally, the transgressions in the cringe condition were rated as more intentional (B = 15.31, SE = 3.69, p < .001) than those in the vicarious embarrassment condition, and participants reported feeling a greater desire to distance themselves from the cringe transgressors than the vicariously embarrassing transgressors (B = 10.10, SE = 3.72, p = .015). However, we found no difference between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in perceptions of humor (B = -5.00, SE = 3.35, p = .18), emotional valence (B = 0.53, SE = 2.36, p = .82), or relevance to social norms (B = 2.83, SE = 3.44, p = .46). Lastly, participants reported feeling the relevant emotion more intensely in the cringe than vicarious embarrassment condition (B = 9.28, SE = 2.59, p = .002)-i.e., participants experienced greater cringe than vicarious embarrassment in response to the scenarios in their respective experimental conditions.

Discussion

Participants' own examples of cringe and vicarious embarrassment differed in ways consistent with our account. Cringe transgressors were seen as acting more intentionally, yet as less aware of how their behavior came across, and they elicited less empathy and sympathy and a stronger desire for distance. The two emotions did not differ in valence, humor, or relevance to norms, suggesting that both arise from similarly unpleasant norm violations but differ in what observers infer about the transgressor. These results demonstrate that cringe may potentially serve a distinct function in social cognition from vicarious embarrassment. In our next study, we further explored the differences between cringe and vicarious embarrassment, focusing primarily on the role of perceived transgressor intent.

Study 5

We had three main goals for our final study. First, we sought to confirm these differences in a preregistered, confirmatory study and test whether the two emotions have distinct consequences for social judgment and behavior-that is, whether cringe is associated with different inferences, attitudes, and behavioral intentions regarding the transgressor. Second, to test whether intent distinguishes the two emotions, we directly manipulated whether transgressions were intentional or accidental. Third, we examined whether cringe is sensitive to the social context of a transgression by manipulating whether transgressions occurred in public or in private. Self-conscious emotions such as embarrassment are felt more intensely when a transgression is public and common knowledge (Soliman, 2024; Thomas et al., 2018), reflecting their role in managing reputation. If cringe functions to support norm enforcement, it should likewise be heightened for public transgressions: Public violations pose a greater threat to shared norms, are more consequential for the transgressor's reputation, and are where social sanctions such as gossip and exclusion are most likely to be applied. We also sought to address a potential confound by asking participants to generate and rate their own example of cringe (or vicarious embarrassment) without providing formal definitions. Doing so allowed us to capture lay perceptions of these two emotions and mitigate concerns that participants were anchoring their responses to the experimenter-provided definitions from Study 4.

Method

Participants

We tested N = 405 participants (52.1% female), aged 18-80 (MAge = 44.8) from Prolific in a preregistered study: https://osf.io/2u3wc/overview?view_only=af15f6d30a124aa0ac716212de0b79e0. Participants were compensated $2.85 for participating in a 17-min survey. We initially recruited 416 participants, but 11 were excluded for failing our inclusion criteria. Sample size was determined using a statistical power simulation with data from Study 4 which found we would have 100% power (95% CI: 99.63, 100%) to detect an effect of emotion condition with N = 400 given the effect size observed in Study 4 for the intent measure.

Design and Procedure

Participants were randomly assigned to either a cringe or vicarious embarrassment condition, an intentional or accidental vignette condition, and to a public or private reputation condition, all between-subjects. In the first part of the experiment, participants received five short scenarios corresponding to their assigned scenario condition (cringe or vicarious embarrassment) and rated each on the intensity of cringe and vicarious embarrassment (e.g., "how much second-hand embarrassment would you feel observing this situation?") using 100-point sliding scales. The scenarios for both scenario conditions drew from the participant generated examples in Study 4.

Participants then received five scenarios corresponding to their assigned scenario condition and answered a series of measures designed to help dissociate cringe from vicarious embarrassment (henceforth dimension measures). These included items measuring empathy, moral wrongness, perceptions of norm violations, beliefs about the transgressor's awareness of their norm violation, attention seeking, transgressor intent, punishment judgments, punishment response appropriateness, and prosocial motivation to help the target (all using 100-point sliding scales; see Measures in Table 3). Participants were then asked to generate their own example scenario of cringe or vicarious embarrassment, depending on their condition assignment, and rated it on the same nine measures.

In the next part of the task, participants received five new, short scenarios detailing different minor transgressions which varied in the intent of the transgressor. In the intent condition, the transgressions in the vignettes were described as intentional (e.g., "someone intentionally laughs too hard at their boss's joke."), while in the accident condition, they were described as unintentional (e.g., "someone unintentionally laughs too hard at their bosses joke").

For each vignette, participants rated their perceptions of cringe and vicarious embarrassment using 100-point sliding scales. Next, participants received the reputation manipulation-they read three vignettes detailing identical social transgressions that only varied in whether they occurred in private (such that no one else witnessed the transgression occur) or publicly (such that everyone nearby witnessed the transgression occur). For each scenario, participants reported how much cringe they would feel observing the situation using the same 100-point sliding scale measure from earlier in the survey. After the reputation vignettes, participants completed our 20item Cringe Scale. Lastly, they also answered an item assessing how much time they spend on various social media platforms, the one-item cringe sensitivity measure, and several demographic questions.

Analysis

We report each of our primary models in Table 4, along with its predictor, outcome, and main result; full model output is reported in the supplement. Analyses were preregistered unless marked as exploratory in Table 4, and all linear mixed-effects models (LMEMs) included a random intercept for participant ID. Although not preregistered, we applied Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) corrections to the eight transgressor evaluation models to control the false discovery rate (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995); all reported p-values for these models are BHcorrected. For the punishment appropriateness models, which included all four appropriateness ratings simultaneously as dependent measures, we estimated the simple effects of scenario condition and the simple slopes of Cringe Scale score within each punishment type using the emmeans package with Holm correction for multiple comparisons (Aickin & Gensler, 1996; Lenth & Piaskowski, 2026). 4 To ensure our results were not influenced by the specific vignettes selected from Study 4, we re-ran the transgressor evaluation and punishment appropriateness models on participants' self-generated examples. For all mediation and path models, we tested whether indirect effects differed from 0 using cluster-robust standard errors to account for repeated ratings within participants.

Our preregistered comparison of path models with and without intent could not be performed as planned because the model without intent was just-identified. We therefore compared the model with intent to one in which the paths from intent to norm violation perceptions and moral wrongness judgments were constrained to 0, using a χ² difference test.

Although we preregistered LMEMs controlling for the random intercepts of participant and vignette identity, after data analysis we determined that these models were underpowered for our central comparison between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. Because the two scenario conditions used different vignettes (five each), treating vignettes as a random factor meant that the condition effect is estimated from just 10 vignettes rather than from 405 participants (Judd et al., 2012). These tests are therefore very conservative and are powered to detect only large differences between the two sets of vignettes (approximately d ≥ 2.0; Westfall et al., 2014). We therefore deviated from our preregistration: We report LMEMs with a random intercept for participant ID here and report the preregistered models with crossed random intercepts for participant and vignette in the supplement (see Study 5 -Results). Because the two sets of models address different questions-whether participants distinguished our particular cringe and vicarious embarrassment vignettes, and whether these differences generalize to cringe and vicarious embarrassment scenarios more broadly-we discuss the results of both in the Study 5 Discussion.

Results

The results of the manipulation check revealed that the scenario condition manipulation was effective at influencing perceptions of the relevant emotions: the cringe vignettes were perceived as more cringe than the vicarious embarrassment vignettes (B = 5.72, SE = 2.26, p = .012), while the vicarious embarrassment vignettes were perceived as more vicariously embarrassing than the cringe vignettes (B = -9.98, SE = 2.52, p < .001), supporting the notion that our stimuli closely correspond to their hypothesized emotion. Next, we examined the characteristics that differ between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. As predicted, participants and verbal confrontation (B = 10.94, SE = 1.68, p < .001) punishment responses were more appropriate for the cringe than the vicarious embarrassment transgressions (see Figure 3). There was no difference between scenario conditions in the appropriateness of no punishment (B = -2.37, SE = 1.68, p = .16). Lastly, and in contrast to our predictions, participants reported the transgressors in the cringe scenarios were significantly more aware of committing a norm violation than those in the vicarious embarrassment scenarios (B = 12.07, SE = 2.02, p < .001).

Participants' self-generated scenarios replicated this pattern for every outcome: Relative to their vicarious embarrassment examples, participants rated their cringe examples as more intentional, attention seeking, norm violating, morally wrong, and deserving of punishment, and as eliciting less empathy and prosocial motivation (all ps < .001; see Study 5 Analyses in the supplement for full model results). As with the experimenter-selected vignettes, active punishments were judged more appropriate for cringe transgressions, whereas the appropriateness of doing nothing did not differ, and cringe transgressors were again judged more aware of their norm violation.

We next examined whether individual differences in cringe sensitivity predicted norm sensitivity and enforcement. The Cringe Scale score did not significantly predict norm violation perceptions (B = 0.80, SE = 0.79, p = .32) but did significantly predict normative punishment judgments (B = 1.72, SE = 0.62, p = .006). Simple slope analyses found that Cringe Scale score was negatively associated with the appropriateness of not punishing (B = -3.53, SE = 0.88, p < .001)-indicating that individuals higher in trait cringe sensitivity viewed non-punishment as less appropriate-and positively predicted appropriateness ratings of gossip (B = 2.23, SE = 0.88, p = .016), social exclusion (B = 2.33, SE = 0.88, p = .016), and verbal confrontation (B = 3.33, SE = 0.88, p < .001), suggesting that individuals high in trait cringe are more likely to approve of sanctioning norm violators.

Examining the effect of the intent manipulation, we found that participants rated the intentional transgressions as significantly higher in cringe than the accidental transgressions (B = 12.54, SE = 2.23, p < .001, d = 0.38). Interestingly, the intentional transgressions were also rated as significantly higher in vicarious embarrassment than the accidental transgressions (B = 4.61, SE = 2.21, p = .038, d = 0.15). However, in support of our hypothesis, we found a significant interaction effect between intent and rating type (B = 7.93, SE = 1.64, p < .001), such that the effect of intent on cringe perceptions was larger than its effect on perceptions of vicarious embarrassment.

We next examined the mediating role of intent in underlying the differences between cringe and vicarious embarrassment. Intent fully mediated the effect of condition on moral wrongness judgments (B = 13.18, SE = 1.50, p < .001; proportion mediated: 1.03) 5 , and partially mediated the effect of condition on norm violation perceptions (B = 9.35, SE = 1.55, p < .001; proportion mediated: 0.41).

We next tested our planned multiple mediation model; however, this model was misspecified (RMSEA = 0.519, CFI = .798, TLI = -1.02, SRMR = 0.120) and thus we did not interpret the model coefficients. In an exploratory model that allowed the residuals of moral wrongness and norm violation to covary, both judgments mediated the effect of intent on prosocial motivation and punishment. Together they accounted for 69.7% (95% CI [47.6%, 91.7%]) of the effect of intent on prosocial motivation and 83.2% (95% CI [73.0%, 93.4%]) of its effect on punishment, with moral wrongness carrying the larger share (52.0% and 63.5%, respectively).

We next tested our path models with and without intent to determine its explanatory value within our system of variables. The model with intent exhibited generally adequate model fit (CFI = 0.987, TLI = 0.952, SRMR = 0.021, RMSEA = 0.078, 90% CI: 0.054, 0.106).

However, the model without intent was just-identified, precluding a comparison of model fit.

The model in which the paths between intent and endogenous variables were constrained to 0 resulted in poor model fit (RMSEA = 0.167, SRMR = 0.130, TLI = 0.780, CFI = 0.912). One result appeared to diverge. Participants in Study 4 judged cringe transgressors as less aware that their behavior was cringe, whereas participants in Study 5 judged them as more aware that they had violated a norm. However, the two items measured different kinds of awareness: Study 4 asked whether targets recognized how their behavior would come across to others, whereas Study 5 asked whether they knew they had broken a norm. Together, these results suggest that cringe transgressors are seen as knowingly breaking norms while remaining oblivious to how their behavior is received, and that perceived intent, rather than unawareness, is the more central feature of cringe.

Not all of these differences generalized beyond our particular vignettes. In our preregistered models, which treated vignettes as well as participants as random effects, cringe vignettes remained more intentional and attention seeking and elicited less empathy and prosocial motivation, and gossip, social exclusion, and verbal confrontation remained more appropriate responses to cringe transgressions. Differences in norm violation, moral wrongness, normative punishment judgments, and norm awareness were no longer significant (all ps ≥ .139), nor were the manipulation checks (ps ≥ .197); effects of the intent manipulation, trait cringe, and reputation condition were unchanged. This divergence is informative. Intent, attention seeking, and empathy separated every cringe vignette from every vicarious embarrassment vignette, whereas only two of the five cringe vignettes were judged clearly morally wrong and deserving of punishment, and these were the two perceived as the most severe norm violations (see Study 5

Analyses in the supplement). Perceived intent thus appears to be a general feature of cringe, whereas moral condemnation and punishment may accompany cringe mainly when the violation is perceived as severe. These latter effects were all in the predicted direction and replicated in participants' self-generated examples, which sample a far larger set of scenarios, but establishing them in general will require sampling more scenarios per condition (e.g., 20 or more; Westfall et al., 2014).

A primary goal of this study was to investigate the role of intent in distinguishing cringe from vicarious embarrassment. When directly manipulating whether a transgression was intentional or not, we found that intentional transgressions were perceived as significantly more cringe than accidental transgressions. Unexpectedly, we found that the intentional transgressions were also perceived as more vicariously embarrassing. Importantly however, there was a significant interaction between intent condition and emotion rating such that the effect of intent on cringe perceptions was substantially larger, over twice the effect size, compared to the effect of intent on vicarious embarrassment perceptions, indicating that transgressor intent may play a larger role in the elicitation of cringe than vicarious embarrassment.

The results of our mediation models highlight the important role intent plays in distinguishing cringe from vicarious embarrassment. First, intent significantly mediated differences between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in both moral wrongness judgments and norm violation perceptions: The cringe scenarios were perceived as more intentional, which in turn was associated with heightened moral wrongness and norm violation perceptions. Second, moral wrongness judgments and norm violation perceptions both mediated the effect of intent on prosocial motivation and normative punishment judgments. Specifically, intent increased moral wrongness judgments and norm violation perceptions, both of which were positively associated with punishment judgments and negatively associated with prosocial motivation to help the transgressor. Because our preregistered model was misspecified, these results come from an exploratory model. Modification indices suggested that adding a residual covariance matrix between norm violation perceptions and moral wrongness to our preregistered model would significantly improve model fit (MI = 481, standardized expected path = 0.48), indicating that these are related constructs that may be difficult to separate in future models. Third, when comparing two nested models-one including intent and one without it among a system of variables including scenario condition, prosocial motivation, punishment, morality, and norm violations-the model including intent fit the data far better, suggesting that intent-based pathways partially account for the differences between cringe and vicarious embarrassment in prosocial motivation and punishment.

Lastly, we found that public exposure intensifies feelings of cringe. Participants reported significantly greater perceptions of cringe when the transgression occurred publicly than privately, suggesting that cringe is sensitive to the reputational and normative stakes of a transgression and consistent with its proposed role in norm enforcement and social signaling.

Together, the findings of Study 5 suggest that cringe differs from vicarious embarrassment in its elicitors and social-cognitive consequences; this difference was primarily in observers' inferences about the transgressor's intent which statistically accounted for differences in how the transgressor was evaluated and treated. scenario condition (cringe, vicarious embarrassment) from Study 5.
